stem: For a dataset of 8 observations, sum of x = 120 and sum of x^2 = 1960. Compute the coefficient of variation (CV). [Given: sqrt(20) ~ 4.47]

per_option_rationale.rationale: Student rounds sqrt(20) to 4 (instead of 4.47), then CV = (4/15) x 100 ~ 26.7%, and further rounds or misreads this as 25%.

Student computes variance = 1960/8 - (120/8)^2 but mistakenly uses 200 for (15)^2 instead of 225, giving variance = 45; then CV = (sqrt(45)/15) x 100 ~ 44.7%, or makes a different slip computing SD ~ 3 and CV = (3/15) x 100 = 20%.
Student uses SD/sum(x) x 100 instead of SD/mean x 100: (4.47/120) x 100 ~ 3.7%, or confuses the formula path arriving at 15%.

explanation_sections.punchline: The shortcut variance formula - sum(x^2)/n minus mean^2 - avoids listing all deviations and flows straight to CV.
explanation_sections.approach: Model: direct computation from raw sums. (1) Compute mean: xbar = sum(x)/n. (2) Compute variance using shortcut: sigma^2 = sum(x^2)/n - xbar^2. (3) SD = sqrt(variance). (4) CV = (SD/xbar) x 100. Givens: n=8, sum(x)=120, sum(x^2)=1960. Execute: xbar=15, sigma^2=245-225=20, SD~4.47, CV~30%.
explanation_sections.lesson: The shortcut variance formula sum(x^2)/n - xbar^2 is the fastest route when raw sums are given. Never skip computing the mean first.
explanation_sections.timing: About 80 seconds. Key setup decision: recognise the shortcut variance formula. Trap: rounding sqrt(20) to 4 gives 25%, not 30%.
